newsitem.title: CHILE: Castro to meet friends and foes in Chile.
newsitem.headline: Castro to meet friends and foes in Chile.

text.p: With admirers and enemies planning street rallies at his every step, Cuban leader Fidel Castro will arrive in Chile on Saturday for a summit of leaders of Latin America, Spain and Portugal.

Castro, making his first visit to Chile since the tumultuous days of the late Marxist President Salvador Allende in 1971, was already the focus of attention at the Sixth Ibero-American summit even before he arrived.

Cuban exiles from Miami and local rightists planned protests against Castro, while Chilean Communists prepared welcome rallies and painted brightly colored murals extolling him on walls around Santiago.
Prominent Cuban dissidents such as Armando Valladares, Huber Matos and Castro's former lieutenant Carlos Montaner have flown to Santiago to drum up opposition.

The leaders of 21 countries are due to attend the summit starting on Sunday including Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres in their first event of this kind.
Organizers hoped Castro would not steal the show. "We don't want the summit to become Fidelized," Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said recently.

"Once the presidents start arriving we will start having a profound and varied dialogue between all of them," said the summit's top organizer, Fabio Vio. Asked if Castro would overshadow the others, he said, "I don't think so."

But the summit's official theme -- "Governability in an Efficient and Participative Democracy" -- has not exactly captivated the Chilean public, while Castro's impending visit revived memories of his controversial month-long stay in 1971 during Allende's leftist government.
Almost exactly 25 years later, Castro will find Chile a radically different place from the farming and mining country in the throes of socialist upheaval he visited in 1971.

Its population has nearly doubled to 14 million, the size of the economy has more than tripled and Santiago bristles with gleaming, ultra-modern skyscrapers. Chile's free-market economy, where even the social security system is private, could hardly mark a sharper contrast with Cuba's communism.
The man who met Castro on his arrival in 1971, Gen. Augusto Pinochet, will not be in town to greet him this time.

Pinochet, who led the bloody 1973 coup that overthrew Allende and then ruled Chile for 17 years with an iron fist, is still commander-in-chief of the army, but he has arranged to be out of Santiago at military exercises in northern Chile during Castro's visit.
Pinochet's absence will deprive the summit of what could have been its climactic moment -- a fleeting encounter between Pinochet, known for his blistering anti-communism, and Castro.
Castro will almost certainly be able to notch up another diplomatic victory at the summit against the unpopular Helms-Burton Act tightening the U.S. embargo on his country.

The summit's final document is sure to condemn the law, which allows U.S. citizens and naturalized Cuban exiles to sue foreigners benefiting from properties confiscated by the Cuban government under Castro's revolution, diplomats said.
And they said the meeting was unlikely to make any call for democratic reforms to Cuba's one-party system, a key demand of U.S. President Bill Clinton.

"The rejection of Helms-Burton is unanimous. It has not even been an issue for debate," said a diplomat at the summit, where officials were drafting the final document. "We've gone as far as we can without coming to an open confrontation with Cuba and making an explicit condemnation of the (Castro) regime."
